title: One of the first particle detectors began as a physicist making clouds in a jar

cover.alt: C. T. R. Wilson’s original cloud chamber in a museum case: a brass and glass cylinder on a wooden stand, connected by tubes to a large glass flask.

body: In 1894, while working on the summit of Ben Nevis, the Scottish physicist Charles Wilson was so taken by an optical effect in the mist that he began building sealed chambers to study clouds. He soon found that ions could act as seeds for water droplets. A fast charged particle crossing air full of vapour leaves a line of ions behind it, droplets condense along that line, and the particle’s invisible path appears as a thin streak of cloud. Wilson perfected the first cloud chamber in 1911 and won half of the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

slides.prompt: Which mountain-top sight first set Scottish physicist Charles Wilson thinking about clouds?
slides.detail: He saw it while working on the summit of Ben Nevis in 1894, and started building chambers to recreate clouds and study their optics.

slides.heading: How a cloud chamber shows a particle

slides.alt: Two round views of a cloud chamber side by side: on the left a spray of thick white straight tracks fanning out from a source; on the right many faint, thin, wiggly tracks.
slides.caption: Left: thick, straight alpha tracks from americium-241. Right: thin, wispy beta tracks from strontium-90.

right.label: Beta particle
right.text: A wispy track that shows more knocks from collisions. In a magnet, opposite charges curve opposite ways.

slides.question: Why do diffusion cloud chambers use alcohol vapour instead of water?
options: It freezes at a lower temperature
It glows when radiation hits it
slides.explanation: Their base plate must be kept colder than −26 °C, often with dry ice or an electric Peltier cooler, and water would freeze. Isopropyl alcohol is the usual choice.
